source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Getting Trapped In or Out of a Trade

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: WeakSpikeQuality
candidates.quote: Bar 17 was a high 1 long setup, but the bull spike had bars with small bodies and tails. This was not a strong bull spike, and therefore the high 1 should fail.
candidates.description: Shared primitive for this chapter: classify the most recent short leg/spike as weak when its bars average a small body relative to their range (prominent tails), as opposed to a strong spike of consecutive large-bodied trend bars.
candidates.pseudocode: avgBody = average(abs(close[0]-open[0]), spikeLookback); avgRangeVal = avgRange(spikeLookback); isWeakSpike = avgBody[0] < weakBodyFraction * avgRangeVal[0];
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar/spike classification used as a setup-quality filter)

complexity.reason: a window average of bar bodies compared against a window average range

notes: weakBodyFraction/spikeLookback are readings of 'small bodies and tails'; Brooks gives no numbers.

candidates.name: FadeBreakoutSignalAfterWeakSpike
candidates.quote: Bar 23 was a high 1 buy setup, but this was not a strong bull spike, so bears shorted at its high... Bar 27 was a high 1 buy setup, but again the spike was not strong. The bars were small and the tails were prominent. Bears shorted at its high.
candidates.description: When a high 1/high 2 buy setup (or low 1/low 2 short setup) follows a weak spike (R32-01), fade it: take the opposite-direction trade at the setup bar's extreme instead of taking the literal with-spike signal.
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop (buy stop for the mirrored low-1/low-2 case) at the setup bar's opposite extreme

complexity.reason: depends on the High1/High2/Low1/Low2 bar-counting setup primitives from earlier chapters, which themselves need pivot/leg-count detection, on top of the weak-spike classification

notes: This is the chapter's central, repeated pattern across nearly every bar in Figure 32.1 (bars 16, 17, 18, 19, 23, 27, 28, 30): a countertrend or with-weak-spike setup is more tradeable faded than taken at face value.

candidates.name: FadeCountertrendSignalDuringStrongOppositeTrend
candidates.quote: Bar 18 was a low 2 short setup, but the market was still in a strong bull channel and now was going sideways for six bars. This low 2 was likely to fail, so bulls bought its low for a scalp... Bar 16 was a low 1 short setup after five bull trend bars and therefore likely to fail. Bulls would have bought at the low of the bar.
candidates.description: A countertrend low 1/low 2 short setup (or high 1/high 2 long setup) that forms while the larger trend is still judged strongly in the opposite direction is likely to fail; fade it (take the with-trend side at the setup bar's extreme) instead of the literal countertrend signal.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'still in a strong bull channel/trend' is a context classification this chapter assumes but does not reduce to a bar-level test
isCountertrendSetup = lowNSetupPrimitive[0]; strongOppositeTrend = strongBullTrendContext[0]; fadeShort = isCountertrendSetup && strongOppositeTrend; allowLongAtSetupLow = fadeShort;
candidates.book_order_type: buy limit/stop at the failing countertrend setup bar's extreme

complexity.reason: "still in a strong trend" is not defined mechanically in this chapter and needs the same always-in/trend-strength design decision flagged elsewhere in this corpus

notes: Overlaps R32-02 conceptually (both fade a setup that 'should' fail); this candidate isolates the specific 'strong opposite trend' reason, as distinct from the 'weak spike' reason.

candidates.name: AvoidSignalNearTradingRangeMidpoint
candidates.quote: Bar 30 was a large doji bear reversal bar and a high 2 buy setup, but it was in the middle of a trading range and the large signal bar forced traders to buy near the top, which is never good.
candidates.description: A reversal/breakout setup located in the middle of an established trading range (not near either edge) is weaker and forces an unfavorable entry price relative to the range; fade or avoid such a setup rather than taking it at face value.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'in the middle of a trading range' needs the range's high/low boundaries identified, which this chapter assumes rather than defines
signalPositionInRange = (setupBarPrice - rangeLow) / (rangeHigh - rangeLow); isNearMidpoint = abs(signalPositionInRange - 0.5) <= midpointTolerance; avoidSetup = isNearMidpoint;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (filters out a setup located near the middle of the established range)

complexity.reason: requires identifying the current trading range's high/low boundaries, a design decision this chapter assumes rather than defines mechanically

candidates.name: DojiSignalBarWeakensSetup
candidates.quote: Bar 30 was a large doji bear reversal bar and a high 2 buy setup... The doji bar was a weak signal bar.
candidates.description: Treat a doji signal bar (a bar whose body is a small fraction of its range) as a weak/low-confidence signal -- appropriate to fade rather than take at face value, especially when the doji is also unusually large.
candidates.pseudocode: signalBarIsDoji = abs(close[1] - open[1]) <= dojiBodyFraction * (high[1] - low[1]); weakSignal = signalBarIsDoji;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar-quality classification used to downgrade or fade a setup)

complexity.reason: single-bar body/range comparison at a fixed lag

notes: A generic doji-bar classification is very likely already defined as a primitive in earlier chapters (trend/bar-pattern chapters); recorded here since this chapter uses it explicitly as a fade reason.

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutBarReversalEntry
candidates.quote: Once the short triggered, alert traders would have bought above bar 2 on a stop, both because there were trapped bears and because the market went above a strong bull trend bar on a gap up day and the day could become a trend from the open bull trend day.
candidates.description: After a bear signal bar triggers a short entry by breaking below a prior strong (opposite-direction) trend bar, if price instead reverses back up above that trend bar's high, enter long on a stop above it -- the 'trapped countertrend traders' reversal entry.
candidates.pseudocode:
priorTrendBarHigh = high[1]; // the strong bull trend bar whose break triggered the now-failing short
enterLongAtStop = open[0] <= priorTrendBarHigh + tick && high[0] > priorTrendBarHigh + tick;
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the prior strong trend bar's high

complexity.reason: needs identifying which recent bar's breakdown triggered the countertrend short that is now failing; here a fixed short lookback (the immediately preceding trend bar), not general pivot detection

notes: Related to the corpus's failed-breakout/failed-reversal-pattern continuation family (see R20-05 in chapter 20), but triggered off a single trend bar rather than a double-top/head-and-shoulders pattern.

rejected.quote: It is simplistic to think that they are all getting it wrong... most will have nothing to do with a 5 minute chart... What appears on the chart is the distilled product of a huge number of traders who are basing their decisions on a huge number of different and unknowable reasons.
rejected.reason: requires knowledge of other market participants' unobservable motives/order flow across timeframes the engine does not have

chapter_summary: A short chapter whose thesis is that both entry stops and protective stops can 'trap' traders, and that a careful reader of price action can profit by fading the setups that are trapping others. Nearly the entire chapter is a single bar-by-bar chart walkthrough (Figure 32.1) restating the same handful of fade conditions over and over: a with-spike breakout/pullback setup (high 1/2, low 1/2) is unreliable when the preceding spike is weak (R32-01/R32-02) or when it runs countertrend to a still-strong larger trend (R32-03), and a setup located in the middle of a trading range or built on a doji signal bar is similarly weak (R32-04/R32-05). R32-06 captures the one distinct pattern in the chapter, a 'trapped countertrend trader' reversal entry off a single failed breakout bar. Because R32-02, R32-03, and R32-04 all lean on context primitives (spike strength, trend strength, trading-range boundaries) that this short chapter uses but does not itself define, several are graded research/hard and should be reconciled with whatever concrete definitions the dedup pass finds in the trend and trading-range chapters that introduce those primitives.
